section_summary: This final section completes the monograph’s account of Japanese activities in Brazil, covering sabotage, secret organizations, espionage, strategic-material purchases, military capabilities, government controls, immigration, agriculture, and commerce. It then reproduces wartime documents from Japan and the United States, followed by Japan’s 1945 surrender authorization, proclamation, and formal Instrument of Surrender. The section concludes with the monograph’s alphabetical index.

subfiles.title: Japanese Monograph—Latin America: Japanese Activities in Brazil
subfiles.about: Continuation of a monograph chapter assessing Japanese sabotage, espionage, organizations, military potential, immigration, agriculture, and commerce in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: The chapter alleges crop destruction, arson, threats, secret organizations, intelligence gathering, passport theft, and contacts among Japanese, German, and Spanish representatives in Brazil. It reviews arrests of alleged Japanese military personnel, purchases of diamonds and quartz crystal, the strategic location of Japanese settlements, and Brazilian controls imposed after the rupture of diplomatic relations. A lengthy quotation from Seizo Mogami’s South America presents Japanese perspectives and statistics on immigration, schools, farming, industry, colonization, and commercial enterprises.

subfiles.title: Appendices I–III: Japanese Declaration of War and United States War Measures
subfiles.from: Emperor of Japan; Franklin D. Roosevelt; Congress of the United States
subfiles.to: Japanese subjects; Congress and people of the United States
subfiles.about: Reproduces Japan’s declaration of war, Roosevelt’s request for a declaration of war, and the congressional resolution declaring war on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Appendix I gives the Japanese imperial rescript declaring war on the United States and British Empire and justifying the decision as one of national survival and East Asian stability. Appendix II reproduces Roosevelt’s account of the attack on Pearl Harbor and simultaneous Japanese operations across the Pacific. Appendix III prints the congressional joint resolution formally recognizing a state of war and authorizing the use of all national military resources.

subfiles.title: Appendix IV: Imperial Authorization and Proclamation of Surrender
subfiles.to: Japanese Imperial Government, Imperial General Headquarters, armed forces, and people of Japan
subfiles.about: Authorizes Yoshijiro Umezu to sign the surrender instrument and commands acceptance and implementation of the Allied surrender terms.
subfiles.summary: The imperial authorization of September 1 empowers Yoshijiro Umezu to sign the Instrument of Surrender for the emperor and Imperial General Headquarters. The proclamation of September 2 accepts the Potsdam terms and orders the Japanese government, armed forces, and people to cease hostilities, disarm, and execute the surrender provisions. Both documents bear Hirohito’s authority and countersignatures from senior military and cabinet officials.

subfiles.title: Appendix V: Instrument of Surrender
subfiles.from: Representatives of the Emperor of Japan, Japanese Government, and Imperial General Headquarters
subfiles.about: Formally records Japan’s unconditional surrender to the Allied Powers and the authority of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers.
subfiles.summary: Japan accepts the Potsdam Declaration, proclaims the unconditional surrender of all Japanese forces, and orders the cessation of hostilities and preservation of military and civil property. The instrument requires obedience to Allied directives, liberation of prisoners and internees, and subordination of imperial governmental authority to the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. It was signed and accepted aboard ship in Tokyo Bay by Japanese and Allied representatives on September 2, 1945.

subfiles.title: Index to Japanese Monograph—Latin America
subfiles.about: Alphabetical index of people, organizations, places, ships, laws, publications, and subjects appearing throughout the monograph.
subfiles.summary: The index runs alphabetically from Aburto through Zinsser and supplies internal monograph page references. Its entries document the geographic breadth of the work and its emphasis on Japanese diplomatic, commercial, immigrant, intelligence, propaganda, and military networks throughout Latin America.
